meta.name: BountyCode Knowledge Corpus
meta.description: Canonical concept registry and prerequisite graph for the BountyCode content factory. Source material is used for curriculum discovery and factual verification only. All generated content is original.

c_basics.title: C Basics
c_basics.definition: C is a compiled, statically typed, procedural language created in the 1970s by Dennis Ritchie. It provides direct memory access and maps closely to machine instructions.
c_basics.mental_model: C is the closest thing to speaking directly to the CPU while still being portable. Every other language eventually touches the same concepts C exposes directly: memory, pointers, and compiled machine code.
key_rules: Every program needs a main() function
Variables must be declared before use
Memory is manually managed with malloc/free
The compiler translates source to machine code before execution
common_mistakes: Buffer overflows from missing bounds checks
edge_cases: Signed integer undefined behavior on overflow
Array decay to pointer in function arguments
debugging_patterns: Use printf debugging for control flow
interview_questions: What is the difference between declaration and definition?
Why does C need a header file?
What happens during preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking?
practice_targets: Write a program that reads input and prints formatted output
Convert temperatures between Celsius and Fahrenheit
Print a right-angled triangle of stars

worked_examples.title: Hello World
worked_examples.explanation: The minimal C program. #include pulls in stdio.h. main() is the entry point. printf prints formatted output. return 0 signals success to the OS.

misconceptions.correction: C powers operating systems, embedded systems, databases, and game engines. Understanding C teaches how computers actually work.
misconceptions.evidence: Linux kernel, Windows kernel, PostgreSQL, Redis, and most embedded firmware are written in C.

misconceptions.misconception: C is just C++ without classes
misconceptions.correction: C and C++ have diverged. C is simpler, more portable, and preferred for systems programming. C++ has RAII, templates, and STL.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 2 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

c_variables.title: C Variables & Data Types
c_variables.definition: Variables are named memory locations that hold values of a specific type. C requires explicit type declarations before use.
c_variables.mental_model: A variable is a labeled box in memory. The type determines the box size and what can be stored inside.
key_rules: Variables must be declared with a type before use
Type determines size and interpretation of bits
int is at least 16 bits, typically 32
float is single precision, double is double precision
common_mistakes: Using a variable before assigning a value
edge_cases: Integer overflow wraps around (unsigned) or is undefined (signed)
debugging_patterns: Use sizeof() to check actual sizes
interview_questions: What is the size of int on your machine?
What is the difference between int and long?
When would you use float vs double?
practice_targets: Write a program that computes the size of each type
Swap two variables using a temporary variable
Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit using float arithmetic

c_pointers.title: C Pointers & Memory
c_pointers.definition: Pointers are variables that store memory addresses. They enable direct memory manipulation, dynamic allocation, and efficient array handling.
c_pointers.mental_model: A pointer is an envelope containing a house address. Dereferencing (*) opens the envelope and goes to the house. The address-of operator (&) writes the house address onto the envelope.
key_rules: * dereferences a pointer to access the value at the address
& gives the address of a variable
Pointers must be typed: int* differs from char*
NULL is the null pointer constant
Dereferencing a null or invalid pointer causes undefined behavior
common_mistakes: Forgetting to allocate memory before use
Pointer arithmetic confusion (p+1 advances by sizeof(type))
Returning address of a local variable
edge_cases: Void pointers require casting before dereferencing
Pointer to pointer (**p) for dynamic 2D arrays
debugging_patterns: Use printf("%p", ptr) to inspect addresses
Use valgrind to detect invalid reads/writes
interview_questions: What is the difference between pass by value and pass by reference?
Why is pointer arithmetic scaled by the data type size?
practice_targets: Write a function that reverses a string in place

worked_examples.title: Swap using pointers
worked_examples.explanation: Parameters are pointers. *a dereferences to access the original variable. Changes through *a affect the caller's variable because we have its address.

misconceptions.correction: Pointers are fundamental to C. Array indexing, pass-by-reference, dynamic memory, and data structures all use pointers.
misconceptions.evidence: Every array operation, function parameter passing by reference, and malloc/free call involves pointers.

misconceptions.misconception: Pointer arithmetic is like integer arithmetic
misconceptions.correction: p + 1 advances by sizeof(*p) bytes, not 1 byte. For int*, p+1 moves 4 bytes. For char*, p+1 moves 1 byte.
misconceptions.evidence: int arr[5]; int *p = arr; (p+1) - p == 1, but (char*)(p+1) - (char*)p == sizeof(int).

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 2 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

c_oop.title: OOP in C
c_oop.definition: C is not an object-oriented language, but OOP concepts can be implemented using structures, function pointers, and encapsulation patterns.
c_oop.mental_model: A struct is a data bag. A struct + function pointers is a class. Opaque pointers hide implementation. Inheritance is manual vtable dispatch.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to initialize vtable in constructor
Confusing struct pointer with struct value semantics
edge_cases: Flexible array members at end of struct
Function pointer casts may break ABI
debugging_patterns: Print vtable addresses to verify dispatch
Use sizeof to check struct layout
interview_questions: Can you implement polymorphism in C?
What is an opaque pointer and why use it?
practice_targets: Implement a Shape hierarchy with area() using function pointers
Build a linked list with OOP-style interface

cpp_basics.title: C++ Basics
cpp_basics.definition: C++ is a multi-paradigm language extending C with classes, templates, RAII, and the Standard Template Library (STL).
cpp_basics.mental_model: C++ is C with a powerful type system and library on top. Start with C thinking, then layer on C++ features.
key_rules: STL containers manage their own memory
interview_questions: What is the difference between C and C++?
What is RAII and why does it matter?
Why does C++ have both struct and class?
practice_targets: Write a simple class with constructor and destructor
Implement a vector wrapper with push_back and size

cpp_stl.title: C++ STL Containers
cpp_stl.definition: The Standard Template Library provides generic containers (vector, list, map, set) and algorithms (sort, find, transform).
cpp_stl.mental_model: STL containers are generic buckets. Choose the right bucket for access patterns: vector for index, list for splice, map for lookup, set for uniqueness.
key_rules: vector: contiguous, O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete middle
list: doubly linked, O(1) splice, no random access
map: red-black tree, O(log n) ordered lookup
unordered_map: hash table, O(1) average lookup
common_mistakes: Using vector for frequent middle insertions
Using map when unordered_map is sufficient
edge_cases: vector<bool> is a bitset specialization, not a true container
string is a contiguous container of char
priority_queue is a heap, not sorted container
debugging_patterns: Reserve vector capacity for known sizes
interview_questions: When would you use list vs vector?
What is the complexity of inserting into the middle of a vector?
practice_targets: Implement a frequency counter using unordered_map
Write a function that merges two sorted vectors

java_basics.title: Java Basics
java_basics.definition: Java is a class-based, object-oriented language designed for portability via the JVM. It features automatic memory management (garbage collection) and a rich standard library.
java_basics.mental_model: Java runs on a virtual machine. Write once, run anywhere. Everything is an object (except primitives). The JVM manages memory automatically.
key_rules: Every application needs a main() method
Primitives: int, long, float, double, char, boolean
edge_cases: Autoboxing cache for small integers (-128 to 127)
interview_questions: What is the difference between == and equals()?
What is the JVM and what does it do?
practice_targets: Write a program that reads a name and prints a greeting
Implement a simple calculator with four operations

java_collections.title: Java Collections Framework
java_collections.definition: The Collections Framework provides interfaces and classes for storing and manipulating groups of objects: List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque.
java_collections.mental_model: Collections are containers. List keeps order and allows duplicates. Set enforces uniqueness. Map stores key-value pairs. Choose based on access pattern.
key_rules: ArrayList: resizable array, O(1) random access
LinkedList: doubly linked, O(1) insert/delete at known position
HashMap: hash table, O(1) average get/put
TreeMap: red-black tree, O(log n) ordered
HashSet: unique elements, backed by HashMap
common_mistakes: Using raw types instead of generics
Forgetting to override hashCode() with equals()
edge_cases: HashMap allows one null key, multiple null values
TreeMap does not allow null keys (natural ordering)
interview_questions: When would you use ArrayList vs LinkedList?
What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable?
practice_targets: Find duplicates in an array using a Set

python_basics.title: Python Basics
python_basics.definition: Python is a high-level, dynamically typed, interpreted language emphasizing readability. It uses indentation for block structure and has a rich standard library.
python_basics.mental_model: Python is executable pseudocode. The interpreter handles memory automatically. Focus on expressing ideas clearly; performance optimization comes later with profiling.
key_rules: The interpreter executes line by line
Colon starts a block, indentation ends it
common_mistakes: Using is instead of == for value comparison
debugging_patterns: Use print() or logging for quick inspection
Use type() and isinstance() to inspect types
interview_questions: What is the GIL and why does it exist?
What are decorators and when would you use them?
practice_targets: Write a function that returns the Fibonacci sequence
Read a file and count word frequencies

worked_examples.title: List comprehension
worked_examples.code: squares = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
worked_examples.explanation: Compact loop that builds a list. for x in range(10) iterates. if x % 2 == 0 filters even numbers. x**2 transforms each element.

misconceptions.correction: Python is fast enough for most applications. Performance-critical paths use C extensions (NumPy, Pandas). Developer productivity often matters more than raw speed.
misconceptions.evidence: Instagram, Spotify, and Dropbox use Python for core services.

misconceptions.correction: Indentation is syntax in Python. It defines block structure. Mixed tabs/spaces cause errors.
misconceptions.evidence: Python will raise IndentationError for inconsistent indentation.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 2 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

python_data_structures.title: Python Data Structures
python_data_structures.definition: Python provides built-in data structures: list, tuple, set, dict. Each has specific performance characteristics and use cases.
python_data_structures.mental_model: Lists are dynamic arrays. Tuples are immutable lists. Sets are unordered unique collections. Dicts are hash maps. Choose based on whether you need order, uniqueness, or keyed access.
key_rules: list: ordered, mutable, allows duplicates, O(1) append
set: unordered, unique elements, O(1) membership test
dict: key-value pairs, O(1) average lookup
All are dynamic, no fixed size declaration
common_mistakes: Using a list when a set would be faster for membership tests
Confusing shallow vs deep copy with copy()
Expecting dicts to maintain insertion order before Python 3.7
edge_cases: set is unhashable, so cannot be a dict key
tuple can be a dict key if elements are hashable
dict preserves insertion order from Python 3.7+
debugging_patterns: Use type() to verify container types
interview_questions: When would you use a list vs a set?
What is the time complexity of dict lookup?
How do you copy a list without aliasing?
practice_targets: Remove duplicates from a list while preserving order
Group words by first letter using defaultdict

javascript_basics.title: JavaScript Basics
javascript_basics.definition: JavaScript is a dynamically typed, prototype-based language primarily used for web development. It runs in browsers and on servers via Node.js.
javascript_basics.mental_model: JavaScript is single-threaded with an event loop. Functions are first-class citizens. Objects are prototype chains, not classes (though class syntax exists).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to return from arrow functions with braces
interview_questions: What is the difference between == and ===?
practice_targets: Write a function that reverses a string
Build a todo list with add/remove/toggle

html_css.title: HTML & CSS Fundamentals
html_css.definition: HTML provides document structure via elements. CSS provides presentation via selectors, properties, and layout models (box model, flexbox, grid).
html_css.mental_model: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin. Elements are boxes. Selectors target boxes. Properties style boxes. Layout models arrange boxes.
key_rules: HTML elements have opening and closing tags
CSS selectors match elements by tag, class, id, or attribute
The box model: content, padding, border, margin
common_mistakes: Using <div> for everything instead of semantic elements
Using inline styles instead of classes
Confusing block, inline, and inline-block display
edge_cases: Z-index only works on positioned elements
Flexbox gap not supported in older browsers
debugging_patterns: Use computed styles to inspect final values
Temporarily add outline: 1px solid red to all elements
interview_questions: What is the difference between flexbox and grid?
How do you center a div horizontally and vertically?
practice_targets: Create a card layout with flexbox

dsa_arrays.title: Arrays
dsa_arrays.definition: Arrays store elements at contiguous memory locations, enabling O(1) random access by index. They are the foundation for most other data structures.
dsa_arrays.mental_model: An array is a row of numbered lockers. You can jump directly to any locker by its number (index). Adding/removing in the middle requires shifting everything after it.
key_rules: 2D arrays store rows of row-length arrays
Slicing creates a view or copy depending on language
common_mistakes: Not checking array bounds (segfault in C, exception in Python/Java)
Creating unnecessary copies of large arrays
edge_cases: Empty array: length 0, no valid indices
Single-element array: first and last are the same
debugging_patterns: Print indices alongside values in loops
interview_questions: How do you reverse an array in place?
What is the time complexity of inserting in the middle?
practice_targets: Find the maximum element in an array
Rotate an array by k positions

worked_examples.title: Two sum with hash map
worked_examples.explanation: Brute force is O(n^2). Hash map reduces to O(n). For each number, check if its complement was seen earlier. seen stores {value: index}.

misconceptions.correction: Random access is O(1), but insertion/deletion in middle is O(n) due to shifting.
misconceptions.evidence: Inserting at index 0 in a 1000-element array requires shifting all 1000 elements.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

dsa_linked_lists.title: Linked Lists
dsa_linked_lists.definition: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node contains data and a reference to the next node. Insertion and deletion are O(1) at known positions.
dsa_linked_lists.mental_model: A linked list is a treasure hunt. Each node is a clue containing data and the location of the next clue. You can only find items by following the chain from the start.
key_rules: Singly linked: each node points to next
Doubly linked: each node points to both next and previous
Insertion/deletion at known position is O(1) once found
common_mistakes: Losing the head pointer during deletion
Not handling empty list edge case
Confusing head/tail in singly vs doubly linked
Forgetting to update next/prev pointers during insertion
edge_cases: Cycles in the list (use Floyd's cycle detection)
debugging_patterns: Draw the list on paper before coding
Use two pointers (slow/fast) for cycle detection
interview_questions: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
How do you reverse a linked list?
What is the difference between singly and doubly linked lists?

worked_examples.title: Reverse linked list
worked_examples.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev
worked_examples.explanation: Classic three-pointer technique. prev tracks reversed portion. curr is current node. nxt saves next before we break the link. Advance all three.

misconceptions.misconception: Linked lists are always better than arrays
misconceptions.correction: Linked lists have O(1) insert/delete at known positions but O(n) search. Arrays have O(1) random access but O(n) middle insertion. Choose based on access pattern.
misconceptions.evidence: If you need index-based access 90% of the time, array is better despite slower insertions.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

dsa_trees.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
dsa_trees.definition: A tree is a hierarchical structure with a root node and child nodes. A binary search tree (BST) maintains the invariant: left child < parent < right child.
dsa_trees.mental_model: A BST is a sorted phone book. To find someone, you open in the middle, go left or right, and repeat. Each step eliminates half the remaining entries.
key_rules: BST: left < parent < right for every node
Inorder traversal of BST gives sorted order
Height-balanced BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n) operations
A node with no children is a leaf
Depth is distance from root, height is distance to deepest leaf
common_mistakes: Forgetting to return values in recursive functions
Infinite recursion from missing base case
edge_cases: Duplicate keys in BST (usually not allowed)
debugging_patterns: Trace recursion with a stack diagram
Print inorder traversal to verify BST property
interview_questions: How do you validate a BST?
What is the time complexity of search in a balanced BST?
How do you find the lowest common ancestor?
practice_targets: Validate if a binary tree is a BST

worked_examples.title: Inorder traversal
worked_examples.explanation: Left subtree, then current node, then right subtree. For BST, this prints values in sorted order.

misconceptions.correction: Binary trees have at most 2 children. B-trees, trie, and segment trees have more. Each type has specific use cases.
misconceptions.evidence: Database indexes use B-trees (many children per node). Autocomplete uses tries (26 children per node).

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

dsa_graphs.title: Graphs
dsa_graphs.definition: A graph is a collection of vertices (nodes) connected by edges. It can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, cyclic or acyclic.
dsa_graphs.mental_model: A graph is a map. Cities are nodes, roads are edges. Some roads are one-way (directed), some have distances (weighted). BFS explores layer by layer. DFS explores one path fully before backtracking.
key_rules: Adjacency list: O(V+E) space, fast for sparse graphs
Adjacency matrix: O(V^2) space, fast edge lookup
BFS: shortest path in unweighted graph
DFS: explores deeply, good for cycle detection
common_mistakes: Using DFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs
Not marking visited nodes in undirected graphs
Confusing directed vs undirected edge addition
debugging_patterns: Trace BFS/DFS with a queue/stack diagram
Count visited nodes vs total nodes
interview_questions: When would you use BFS vs DFS?
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
What is topological sort and when is it used?
practice_targets: Find shortest path between two nodes

worked_examples.title: BFS shortest path
worked_examples.explanation: BFS explores level by level. queue stores (node, distance). When we reach end, dist is shortest path length in unweighted graph.

misconceptions.correction: DFS explores deeply first. It may find a path but not necessarily the shortest. BFS guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.
misconceptions.evidence: In a graph where shortest path is A->B->C (2 hops) but DFS goes A->D->E->F->C (4 hops), DFS returns longer path.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

dsa_dp.title: Dynamic Programming
dsa_dp.definition: Dynamic Programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and storing results in a table (memoization or tabulation).
dsa_dp.mental_model: DP is recursion with memory. If you'd solve the same subproblem twice, store the answer. The table replaces the recursion tree with a grid of computed values.
key_rules: Define state: what does dp[i] represent?
Find recurrence: dp[i] depends on which previous states?
debugging_patterns: Print the DP table after filling
interview_questions: When should you use DP vs greedy?
Explain the knapsack problem and its DP solution
How do you know if a problem has optimal substructure?

worked_examples.title: Fibonacci with memoization
worked_examples.explanation: Naive fib is O(2^n). Memoization caches results. lru_cache decorator handles caching automatically. Each fib(n) computed once. Total O(n).

misconceptions.misconception: DP is only for optimization problems
misconceptions.correction: DP solves any problem with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Counting, decision, and search problems can use DP.
misconceptions.evidence: Counting paths in grid, determining if string is interleaving of two others, and finding longest common subsequence all use DP.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

dbms_sql.title: SQL & Databases
dbms_sql.definition: SQL is a declarative language for querying and manipulating relational data. A DBMS stores, retrieves, and manages data in structured tables with schemas.
dbms_sql.mental_model: A database is a spreadsheet with superpowers. Tables are sheets. Rows are records. Columns are fields. JOINs merge sheets. Indexes are the table of contents.
key_rules: SELECT retrieves columns, FROM specifies tables
JOIN combines tables on related columns
GROUP BY aggregates rows with same values
common_mistakes: Confusing INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN
Not using indexes on filtered columns
edge_cases: NULL handling in comparisons (use IS NULL)
debugging_patterns: Run EXPLAIN to inspect query plan
Test with edge case data (empty tables, NULLs)
interview_questions: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
How do you find the second highest salary?
What is normalization and why does it matter?
practice_targets: Write a query to find duplicate emails
Find the top 3 salaries per department

worked_examples.title: Find second highest salary
worked_examples.code: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
worked_examples.explanation: Subquery finds highest salary. Outer query finds maximum salary less than that. Result is second highest.

misconceptions.correction: SQL includes DDL (CREATE, ALTER), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DCL (GRANT, REVOKE), and TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK).
misconceptions.evidence: Database administrators spend most of their time on schema design (DDL) and performance tuning, not just SELECT queries.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

os_processes.title: Operating Systems: Processes & Threads
os_processes.definition: A process is an executing program with its own memory space. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process, sharing memory with other threads in the same process.
os_processes.mental_model: A process is a house. Threads are people living in the house. Each person has their own room (stack) but shares the kitchen and living room (heap, code, data).
key_rules: Process: independent memory space, heavy context switch
Thread: shared memory within process, lightweight context switch
Race condition: two threads modify shared data concurrently
edge_cases: Thread creation overhead on different OS
interview_questions: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
practice_targets: Implement a thread-safe counter with mutex
Detect deadlock in a resource allocation graph

networking_basics.title: Computer Networking Basics
networking_basics.definition: Computer networking enables devices to communicate via protocols. The Internet uses TCP/IP as the foundational protocol suite.
networking_basics.mental_model: Networking is postal service for data. Packets are letters. IP addresses are house addresses. Ports are apartment numbers. TCP guarantees delivery; UDP is postcards.
key_rules: DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses
common_mistakes: Confusing TCP and UDP use cases
debugging_patterns: Use curl -v to inspect HTTP requests
Use tcpdump or Wireshark for packet capture
interview_questions: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
What happens when you type a URL in a browser?
practice_targets: Build a simple HTTP client with socket

worked_examples.title: HTTP request lifecycle
worked_examples.code:
# 1. DNS resolution: google.com -> 142.250.80.46
# 2. TCP handshake: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
# 3. HTTP request: GET / HTTP/1.1
# 4. Server processes and sends response
# 5. TCP teardown: FIN -> ACK -> FIN -> ACK
worked_examples.explanation: Every web request follows this flow. DNS translates domain to IP. TCP establishes connection. HTTP sends request. Server responds. Connection closes.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP is the only web protocol
misconceptions.correction: HTTP is application layer. Below it: TCP (transport), IP (network), Ethernet (link). Above it: WebSocket, gRPC, GraphQL.
misconceptions.evidence: WebSocket upgrades HTTP connection for real-time communication. gRPC uses HTTP/2 for RPC calls.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

git_basics.title: Git Version Control
git_basics.definition: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to files over time, enabling collaboration, branching, and history recovery.
git_basics.mental_model: Git is a time machine for code. Each commit is a snapshot. Branches are parallel timelines. Merging combines timelines. Remotes are backup time machines on other computers.
key_rules: Branches are lightweight pointers to commits
HEAD points to the current branch/commit
Remotes sync local and remote repositories
edge_cases: Merge conflicts when same lines changed
debugging_patterns: Use git log --graph --oneline to visualize history
Use git diff to inspect changes
Use git status to see current state
interview_questions: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
What is a conflict and how do you resolve it?
Explain the git workflow for a feature branch
practice_targets: Create a repo, make commits, create branches, merge
Write a .gitignore for a Python project

worked_examples.title: Feature branch workflow
worked_examples.code:
# Start feature
git checkout -b feature/user-auth
# Make changes
git add .
git commit -m "Add login form"
# Update with main
git pull origin main --rebase
# Push
git push origin feature/user-auth
worked_examples.explanation: Create branch from main. Make commits. Rebase on latest main to resolve conflicts early. Push for review.

misconceptions.correction: Git is collaboration tool. Branching, merging, and pull requests enable team development. History tells the story of why changes were made.
misconceptions.evidence: git blame shows who changed each line. git log --graph shows branching and merging patterns.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

docker_basics.title: Docker Containers
docker_basics.definition: Docker packages applications and dependencies into lightweight, portable containers that run consistently across environments.
docker_basics.mental_model: A container is a shipping container for code. It bundles the app + runtime + libraries + config. It runs the same on your laptop, the test server, and production.
key_rules: Container: running instance of an image
Dockerfile: recipe for building an image
Containers are isolated but share the host kernel
common_mistakes: Storing secrets in Dockerfiles or images
debugging_patterns: Use docker logs to inspect output
Use docker exec to enter running container
Use docker history to inspect image layers
interview_questions: What is the difference between a container and a VM?
What is a Dockerfile and what does each instruction do?
How do you reduce Docker image size?
practice_targets: Write a Dockerfile for a Python Flask app
Use multi-stage build to reduce image size
Run a container with a volume mount

worked_examples.title: Dockerfile for Python app
worked_examples.code:
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
worked_examples.explanation: FROM sets base image. WORKDIR sets working directory. COPY requirements and install. COPY app code. CMD sets default command.

misconceptions.correction: Containers share the host kernel. VMs virtualize hardware. Containers are processes with isolation. Faster startup, less overhead.
misconceptions.evidence: A container starts in milliseconds. A VM takes minutes. A container uses MBs. A VM uses GBs.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

sql_basics.title: SQL Fundamentals
sql_basics.definition: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases. It supports data definition (DDL), manipulation (DML), and querying (DQL).
sql_basics.mental_model: SQL is asking questions of your data. SELECT asks what you want. FROM says where to look. WHERE filters. JOIN combines related tables. GROUP BY summarizes.
key_rules: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition
JOIN combines tables ON related columns
GROUP BY aggregates rows with same values
ORDER BY sorts the result set
common_mistakes: Not using indexes on WHERE/JOIN columns
edge_cases: NULL handling with IS NULL, not = NULL
debugging_patterns: Run EXPLAIN to check query plan
Test with LIMIT to inspect sample rows
Check for NULLs with IS NULL
interview_questions: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
How do you find the second highest salary?
What are the different types of JOINs?
practice_targets: Find duplicate emails in a table

behavioral_interview.title: Behavioral Interview Mastery
behavioral_interview.definition: Behavioral interviews assess past experiences and soft skills using structured frameworks like STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result).
behavioral_interview.mental_model: Every answer is a mini story with a beginning (situation), middle (action), and end (result). Quantify results. Show growth.
key_rules: Show, don't tell: use specific examples
common_mistakes: Blaming others in team conflict stories
edge_cases: When you failed: show learning, not excuses
When you disagreed with a manager: show diplomacy and data-driven persuasion
When the project failed: focus on what you learned
debugging_patterns: Record yourself answering and listen back
Check if every story has measurable outcomes
interview_questions: Tell me about a time you handled a tight deadline
Describe a conflict with a teammate and how you resolved it
Tell me about a time you failed and what you learned
practice_targets: Practice answering 'Why this company?' with specific research
Prepare a 30-second and 2-minute version of each story

aptitude_quantitative.title: Quantitative Aptitude
aptitude_quantitative.definition: Quantitative aptitude measures numerical reasoning, arithmetic, algebra, and data interpretation skills used in placement tests.
aptitude_quantitative.mental_model: Aptitude math is speed + accuracy. Most problems have a shortcut. Recognize the pattern, apply the formula, verify with estimation.
key_rules: Percentages: x% of y = y% of x
Profit/Loss: CP, SP, profit%, loss% relationships
Ratios: a:b = a/b, combine ratios via LCM
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert units (km/h to m/s)
edge_cases: Successive percentage changes are not additive
interview_questions: A shopkeeper gives 20% discount and still makes 10% profit. Find markup percentage.
If A can do a work in 10 days and B in 15 days, how long together?
practice_targets: Complete a timed set of 30 problems in 45 minutes

system_design_basics.title: System Design Fundamentals
system_design_basics.definition: System design is the process of defining architecture, components, interfaces, and data for a system that meets specified requirements. It balances scalability, reliability, availability, and consistency.
system_design_basics.mental_model: System design is Lego for adults. Start with requirements. Choose components (load balancer, cache, database, queue). Connect them. Identify bottlenecks. Iterate.
key_rules: CAP theorem: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance - pick 2
Load balancers distribute traffic across servers
Caches reduce database load for hot data
Message queues decouple producers and consumers
CDNs cache static content close to users
common_mistakes: Over-engineering for scale you don't have
edge_cases: Eventual consistency vs strong consistency trade-offs
interview_questions: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly
Design a chat application like WhatsApp
How would you design a rate limiter?
practice_targets: Design a URL shortener with 100M users

worked_examples.title: URL shortener design
worked_examples.code:
# Components:
# 1. Client -> Load Balancer
# 2. Load Balancer -> API Servers (stateless)
# 3. API Servers -> Cache (Redis) for hot URLs
# 4. API Servers -> Database (PostgreSQL) for persistence
# 5. Background job -> Cleanup expired URLs
worked_examples.explanation: Stateless API servers scale horizontally. Cache reduces database load for hot URLs. Database persists mappings. Background job handles cleanup.

misconceptions.misconception: System design is about technology choices
misconceptions.correction: System design is about trade-offs. Every choice has costs. CAP theorem: pick 2 of 3. There are no perfect solutions, only appropriate ones.
misconceptions.evidence: Choosing consistency over availability means some users see errors during partitions. Choosing availability means some users see stale data.

verification.verification_notes: Enriched with 1 worked examples, 1 misconceptions, 3 transfer targets.

c_io.title: C Input/Output
c_io.definition: C provides formatted I/O via stdio.h: printf(), scanf(), and file I/O via fopen(), fprintf(), fscanf().
c_io.mental_model: printf is a type-safe messenger needing format specifiers. scanf reads using the same specifiers.
interview_questions: Why does scanf need & for int but not arrays?
practice_targets: Read name and age with scanf

c_dynamic_memory.title: C Dynamic Memory Allocation
c_dynamic_memory.definition: Dynamic memory allocation uses malloc(), calloc(), realloc(), and free() from stdlib.h.
c_dynamic_memory.mental_model: Dynamic memory is self-storage. malloc asks heap for a box. free() returns it. Forgetting free causes leaks.
key_rules: Never free twice or access after free

c_file_io.title: C File I/O
c_file_io.definition: C file I/O uses FILE* streams: fopen, fprintf/fscanf for formatted, fread/fwrite for binary.
c_file_io.mental_model: A file is a stream of bytes. fopen opens a channel. fprintf writes formatted text. fwrite writes raw bytes. fclose shuts the channel.
key_rules: Modes: r, w, a, r+, w+, a+, rb, wb
edge_cases: fseek beyond end undefined for text

cpp_io.title: C++ Input/Output
cpp_io.definition: C++ uses iostream (cin, cout) for type-safe stream-based I/O.
cpp_io.mental_model: Streams are conveyor belts. << sends to cout. >> receives from cin. Compiler checks types.

cpp_arrays.title: C++ Arrays & Vectors
cpp_arrays.definition: C++ provides C-style arrays and std::vector (dynamic array). std::vector manages memory and provides bounds-checked access.
cpp_arrays.mental_model: std::vector is a smart array that grows automatically. Remembers size, manages memory, indexable like C array. Default choice.
common_mistakes: Using C arrays when vector safer

cpp_strings.title: C++ Strings
cpp_strings.definition: std::string is a dynamic, mutable sequence of characters with automatic memory management.
cpp_strings.mental_model: std::string is a smart char array. No manual allocation. Grows as needed. Concatenate, compare, search safely.

cpp_oop.title: C++ OOP
cpp_oop.definition: C++ OOP uses classes with encapsulation, constructors/destructors, inheritance, and virtual functions for polymorphism.
cpp_oop.mental_model: Class is blueprint. Object is building. Inheritance is specialized blueprint. Virtual functions call right method without knowing exact type.
edge_cases: Virtual functions in constructors don't dispatch

cpp_iterators.title: C++ Iterators
cpp_iterators.definition: Iterators abstract container traversal. Categories: input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access.
cpp_iterators.mental_model: Iterator is universal remote for containers. Works on vectors, lists, sets, maps with same interface. ++ advances. * dereferences.

cpp_algorithms.title: C++ STL Algorithms
cpp_algorithms.definition: <algorithm> provides generic algorithms on iterator ranges: sort, find, transform, accumulate.
cpp_algorithms.mental_model: Algorithms are factory machines. Feed iterator range (raw materials) and comparator (blueprint). Get sorted data, found items, or transformed results.
key_rules: find returns end() if not found
practice_targets: Sort vector of structs by field

java_exceptions.title: Java Exceptions
java_exceptions.definition: Java exceptions separate error handling from normal flow. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared.
java_exceptions.mental_model: Exceptions are emergency signals. Checked = red alert (must handle). Runtime = programming bug. try-with-resources is automatic cleanup.

java_streams.title: Java Streams API
java_streams.definition: Streams enable functional-style operations: filter, map, reduce, collect. Intermediate ops lazy, terminal ops eager.
java_streams.mental_model: Stream is assembly line. Items on belt. Intermediate ops (filter, map) are stations. Terminal op (collect, reduce) produces final product.
common_mistakes: Parallel stream on shared mutable state

java_threads.title: Java Threads & Concurrency
java_threads.definition: Java threads enable concurrent execution via Thread/Runnable. synchronized and locks ensure thread safety.
java_threads.mental_model: Threads are workers in factory. Each has own task. Share factory floor (heap). synchronized doors ensure one worker at a time.
key_rules: Thread via extends or implements Runnable
edge_cases: Daemon threads exit when only daemons remain

java_jvm.title: JVM & Memory Management
java_jvm.definition: The JVM executes bytecode with automatic garbage collection. Understanding memory regions helps diagnose performance.
java_jvm.mental_model: JVM is container. Stack = method calls (temporary). Heap = objects (GC-managed). Method area = class metadata. GC sweeps unreachable objects.

python_control_flow.title: Python Control Flow
python_control_flow.definition: Python uses indentation-based blocks: if/elif/else, for/while, match (3.10+), and comprehensions.
python_control_flow.mental_model: Indentation instead of braces. Colons start blocks. Comprehensions are compact loops building collections.

python_oop.title: Python OOP
python_oop.definition: Python OOP uses classes with self, inheritance, property decorators, and dunder methods for operator overloading.
python_oop.mental_model: Class is blueprint with methods. self is instance. Inheritance is is-a. Dunder methods (__str__, __lt__) let objects work with operators.

python_async.title: Python Async Programming
python_async.definition: asyncio enables async programming with coroutines (async def), await, event loop, and tasks for concurrent I/O-bound work.
python_async.mental_model: Async is single waiter managing multiple orders. While waiting for one I/O, start next. asyncio is waiter. async def is order ticket.

python_testing.title: Python Testing
python_testing.definition: Python testing uses unittest (built-in), pytest (preferred), and doctest. TDD writes tests before code.
python_testing.mental_model: Testing is safety net. unittest is built-in net. pytest is better net. Each test is proof code works.
key_rules: pytest: test_* functions or TestCase classes
interview_questions: How test function that raises exception?

javascript_objects.title: JavaScript Objects & Prototypes
javascript_objects.definition: JavaScript objects are key-value collections. Prototypes enable inheritance via prototype chain.
javascript_objects.mental_model: JS object is dictionary. When key not found, check prototype (parent dictionary). class is syntactic sugar over prototype.

javascript_dom.title: JavaScript DOM Manipulation
javascript_dom.definition: The DOM represents HTML as a tree of nodes. JavaScript manipulates via selectors, event listeners, property updates.
javascript_dom.mental_model: DOM is family tree of HTML elements. getElementById finds by ID. querySelector uses CSS selectors. Event listeners are doorbells.

javascript_async.title: JavaScript Async Programming
javascript_async.definition: JavaScript async uses callbacks, Promises, async/await for non-blocking I/O. Event loop manages call stack and task queue.
javascript_async.mental_model: JS is single chef (event loop). Orders queued. While waiting for oven (I/O), start next order. Promises are order tickets. async/await is synchronous recipe writing.
edge_cases: Resolution is async even for resolved

javascript_es6.title: JavaScript ES6+ Features
javascript_es6.definition: ES6+ added let/const, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, spread/rest, modules, classes.
javascript_es6.mental_model: ES6+ is JS growing up. let/const fix scoping. Arrow functions simplify callbacks. Destructuring unpacks. Modules organize. Classes make OOP familiar.

dsa_strings.title: String Algorithms
dsa_strings.definition: String algorithms: pattern matching, searching, manipulation. Techniques: sliding window, KMP, Z-algorithm, rolling hash.
dsa_strings.mental_model: Strings are character arrays with extra tricks. Rolling hash for O(1) substring compare. KMP avoids redundant compares. Sliding window for subarrays.
key_rules: KMP precomputes LPS for O(n) search
Frequency arrays O(1) space for alphabet

dsa_stacks.title: Stacks & Queues
dsa_stacks.definition: Stack: LIFO with push/pop. Queue: FIFO with enqueue/dequeue. Array-based or linked-list-based.
dsa_stacks.mental_model: Stack is stack of plates (last on, first off). Queue is ticket line (first in, first served).
key_rules: Queue: enqueue/dequeue O(1) with linked list

dsa_bst.title: Binary Search Trees
dsa_bst.definition: BST maintains invariant: left < parent < right. Balanced BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n) operations.
dsa_bst.mental_model: BST is sorted phone book that stays sorted. Find: open middle, go left/right, repeat. Inorder = sorted order.

dsa_heaps.title: Heaps & Priority Queues
dsa_heaps.definition: Heap is complete binary tree with heap property: max-heap (parent >= children) or min-heap (parent <= children). Implemented as array.
dsa_heaps.mental_model: Heap is priority queue in tree. Most important always at top. Complete (filled left-to-right) so fits in array perfectly.

dsa_dfs.title: Depth-First Search
dsa_dfs.definition: DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Used for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.
dsa_dfs.mental_model: DFS is exploring a maze. Go left until wall, backtrack, try right. Stack tracks path. Mark visited to avoid loops.
common_mistakes: Confusing DFS tree with actual graph
debugging_patterns: Use iterative to avoid stack overflow
practice_targets: All paths from source to target

dsa_shortest_path.title: Shortest Path Algorithms
dsa_shortest_path.definition: Shortest path algorithms find minimum-cost paths: BFS (unweighted), Dijkstra (non-negative), Bellman-Ford (negative weights), Floyd-Warshall (all pairs).
dsa_shortest_path.mental_model: Shortest path is GPS navigation. BFS is counting blocks (unweighted). Dijkstra is GPS with distances (non-negative). Bellman-Ford handles negative roads (but detects negative cycles).
key_rules: Dijkstra: non-negative weights, O((V + E) log V) with heap
Negative cycle: no shortest path exists
common_mistakes: Confusing shortest path tree with actual paths
Forgetting to initialize distances to infinity
debugging_patterns: Print distance array after each iteration
interview_questions: Time complexity of Dijkstra with heap?

dsa_backtracking.title: Backtracking Algorithms
dsa_backtracking.definition: Backtracking explores all possible solutions recursively, abandoning paths that violate constraints. Used for permutation, combination, subset problems.
dsa_backtracking.mental_model: Backtracking is trying all paths in a maze. When you hit a dead end, backtrack to last choice point and try different path. Abandon paths that can't lead to solution.
key_rules: Base case: solution found or no more choices

dsa_tries.title: Tries (Prefix Trees)
dsa_tries.definition: A trie stores strings by shared prefixes. Each node represents a character. Efficient for prefix-based operations: autocomplete, spell check.
dsa_tries.mental_model: Trie is organized filing cabinet. Each drawer is a letter. Inside are sub-drawers for next letters. 'cat' and 'car' share 'ca' drawer. Fast prefix lookup.
key_rules: Each node has children for next chars
Insert/search/delete: O(L) where L = word length
Space: O(N * L) for N words of avg length L
common_mistakes: Confusing node count with string count
edge_cases: Delete word that's prefix of another
interview_questions: What is a trie and when use it?

dsa_greedy.title: Greedy Algorithms
dsa_greedy.definition: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, hoping for global optimum. Works when problem has greedy-choice property.
dsa_greedy.mental_model: Greedy is always taking the best immediate option. Like always picking the biggest bill when making change (if denominations allow). Fast but not always correct.
key_rules: Make locally optimal choice at each step
Works if problem has greedy-choice property
Often O(n log n) due to sorting
Proof by exchange argument or matroid theory
If in doubt, compare with DP
common_mistakes: Applying greedy when problem needs DP
Greedy works for examples but not all cases
edge_cases: Problems that look greedy but aren't (knapsack)
When greedy fails but DP works
debugging_patterns: Compare greedy result with DP brute force

dsa_intervals.title: Interval Scheduling & Merging
dsa_intervals.definition: Interval problems involve ranges [start, end]. Key operations: merge overlapping, find gaps, schedule non-overlapping, insert new interval.
dsa_intervals.mental_model: Intervals are time slots on a calendar. Merge overlapping meetings. Find free slots between meetings. Schedule max non-overlapping meetings (earliest finish first).
key_rules: Sort by start time for merging
Sort by end time for scheduling (greedy)
Overlap: a.start < b.end AND b.start < a.end
Insert: find position, merge if needed

dsa_sorting.title: Sorting Algorithms
dsa_sorting.definition: Sorting arranges elements in order. Key algorithms: bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick, heap, counting, radix, bucket.
dsa_sorting.mental_model: Sorting is organizing a messy bookshelf. Bubble sort swaps adjacent books repeatedly (slow). Merge sort splits into piles, sorts each, merges (fast). Quick sort picks pivot, partitions, recurses.
key_rules: Comparison sort lower bound: O(n log n)
Merge sort: guaranteed O(n log n), stable, O(n) space
Quick sort: average O(n log n), worst O(n^2), in-place
Heap sort: O(n log n), in-place, not stable
common_mistakes: Not handling duplicates in quicksort (Lomuto vs Hoare)
interview_questions: When use merge sort vs quick sort?

dbms_normalization.title: Database Normalization
dbms_normalization.definition: Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies. Normal forms: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF.
dbms_normalization.mental_model: Normalization is organizing a filing cabinet. 1NF: each field has one value. 2NF: no partial dependency on part of key. 3NF: no transitive dependency on non-key. BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.
common_mistakes: Confusing functional dependency with foreign key
debugging_patterns: Check each normal form in order

dbms_indexing.title: Database Indexing
dbms_indexing.definition: Indexes accelerate data retrieval. Types: B-tree (default), hash (equality), composite (multi-column), covering (includes all needed columns).
dbms_indexing.mental_model: Index is book's table of contents. Without it, read every page (full scan). With it, jump to section. B-tree is balanced tree. Hash is direct lookup. Composite indexes need leftmost prefix.
key_rules: B-tree: O(log n) range and equality
edge_cases: Index on NULL values (usually not indexed)
Function on column prevents index use
debugging_patterns: Run EXPLAIN to see index usage
interview_questions: What is an index and how does it work?
When would you NOT use an index?
What is the leftmost prefix rule?

dbms_transactions.title: Database Transactions & ACID
dbms_transactions.definition: Transactions are atomic units of work. ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE.
dbms_transactions.mental_model: Transaction is a protected box. Either everything inside succeeds and becomes visible (commit), or nothing does (rollback). ACID ensures this promise even with concurrent users.
key_rules: Isolation levels trade safety for performance
interview_questions: What is a deadlock and how prevent it?

os_concurrency.title: Operating Systems: Concurrency
os_concurrency.definition: Concurrency manages multiple executing processes/threads. Synchronization primitives: mutex, semaphore, monitor, condition variable.
os_concurrency.mental_model: Concurrency is multiple workers sharing tools. Mutex is a lock on a tool (only one worker at a time). Semaphore is a pool of identical tools (N workers). Deadlock is when each worker holds a tool the other needs.
key_rules: Deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait

networking_rest.title: REST API Design
networking_rest.definition: REST is architectural style for networked applications. Resources identified by URIs, manipulated via HTTP methods, represented in JSON.
networking_rest.mental_model: REST is a filing system. Each document is a resource (URI). GET reads. POST creates new. PUT updates. DELETE removes. JSON is the document format.

git_branching.title: Git Branching & Merging
git_branching.definition: Git branches enable parallel development. Merge combines branches. Rebase replays commits. Both have trade-offs.
git_branching.mental_model: Branches are parallel timelines. Merge is joining timelines (preserves both histories). Rebase is rewriting timeline to be linear (cleaner but rewrites history).
key_rules: Rebase: replay commits on new base
interview_questions: What is a conflict and how resolve?

git_collaboration.title: Git Collaboration Workflows
git_collaboration.definition: Collaboration workflows: feature branching, Git Flow, trunk-based development. Pull requests enable code review.
git_collaboration.mental_model: Git collaboration is team writing. Feature branch = individual draft. Pull request = asking for review. Main branch = published book. CI = automated proofreading.
edge_cases: Rebase before merge to avoid merge commits
debugging_patterns: git blame to see who changed line
interview_questions: How handle merge conflicts in team?

docker_compose.title: Docker Compose
docker_compose.definition: Docker Compose defines multi-container applications in YAML. Services, networks, and volumes are declaratively configured.
docker_compose.mental_model: Docker Compose is a recipe book. Each service is a dish (web server, database, cache). docker-compose.yml is the recipe. docker-compose up cooks everything.
key_rules: build or image for each service
common_mistakes: Not using named volumes for persistence
Confusing depends_on with actual health checks
Running multiple services in one container
debugging_patterns: docker compose exec to enter container

ci_cd.title: CI/CD Pipelines
ci_cd.definition: CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests on every commit. CD (Continuous Deployment/Delivery) automatically deploys passing builds.
ci_cd.mental_model: CI is automated quality check on every save. CD is automated publishing when quality passes. Pipeline is assembly line: build -> test -> deploy.
key_rules: CI: build + test on every commit
CD: deploy automatically after CI passes
debugging_patterns: Check CI logs for failure point
